title: How to Disciple One Person Over Coffee
excerpt: Not everyone needs a table of twelve. Sometimes discipleship is one person, one standing appointment, and a long obedience built one cup at a time.
body:
Not all discipleship happens around a crowded table. Some of the deepest work God does in a person happens across a small table for two, over coffee that goes cold while two people talk about things that matter. Paul did this. "What you have heard from me," he told Timothy, "entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2). That is one man pouring into one man, who will pour into others. It is the oldest pattern there is.

If the idea of hosting a group feels like too much, start here. One person. One standing appointment. A friendship with a spine of intention running through it.

## Choose the one

Don't overthink who. Look for someone a step or two behind you who is hungry to grow, a newer believer, a younger man or woman, the friend who keeps asking the real questions. Jesus chose twelve, but within the twelve he gave the most to three, and within the three he gave the most to one. Depth is not spread evenly, and that is not favoritism. It is how formation works.

Look for faithfulness more than talent. Paul told Timothy to entrust the gospel to faithful people, not impressive ones. The flashy person who burns hot and disappears will break your heart. The steady person who keeps showing up will outlast you. Pick the steady one.

## Make it a standing appointment

The single most important decision is to make it regular and fixed. Every other Tuesday at 7 a.m. The first Saturday of the month. Whatever rhythm you can both actually keep. A friendship that depends on someone remembering to reach out will quietly die. A standing appointment outlasts your moods and your busy weeks because it does not require either of you to initiate. You just both show up.

Protect it the way you'd protect anything that matters. The slow accumulation of kept appointments is the whole thing. Discipleship is less an event than a long obedience in the same direction, and the standing appointment is what makes the long part possible.

## Have a simple plan, and let it bend

You don't need a curriculum, but you need something to do, or coffee becomes mere catch-up. The simplest plan: read the same short passage or a chapter of a good book between meetings, and talk about it. Or walk slowly through a book of the Bible, a bit at a time, asking what it says about God, about us, and about this week. Or follow whatever the person is actually wrestling with, doubt, a hard marriage, a sin they can't beat, and bring Scripture to bear on it.

The plan exists so you are not aimless. But hold it loosely. Some mornings the person arrives carrying something heavy, and the plan should yield to the person every time. You are discipling a human being, not covering material.

## Ask the questions that go past the surface

Most relationships never get past "how's work." Discipleship has to. Learn a few questions that open the deeper rooms and ask them without flinching. How is your soul, honestly? Where do you feel far from God right now? What sin are you fighting, and how is the fight going? Who knows the real you?

These questions feel intrusive the first time and become a gift over time. They tell the other person that someone is paying attention to the part of them no one else asks about. "Iron sharpens iron," the proverb says, "and one man sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). Sharpening involves friction. The questions are the friction.

## Let them see your life, not just your answers

The coffee table is not a lecture. It is a window. The most formative thing you offer is not your knowledge but your honesty about your own walk, your failures, your repentance, the places you're still being changed. Paul could say, "Follow my example, as I follow the example of Christ" (1 Corinthians 11:1), not because he was finished but because he let people watch him follow.

So confess your own struggles, in proportion and wisdom. The person you're discipling needs to see that the Christian life is not arrival but a continual returning. If you only ever show them a polished version, you teach them to hide their unpolished one. Self-implication is not just a writing move. It is how trust gets built across a coffee table.

## Aim them at someone else

From early on, plant the expectation that this is not the end of the line. The goal is not to create a permanent dependent who needs you to grow. The goal is a disciple who will one day disciple someone else. Say it out loud: "Someday you'll be doing this for somebody else." Paul's instruction to Timothy had four generations in a single verse, Paul to Timothy to faithful people to others. If your discipleship stops with the person across the table, you've made a friend, which is good. But you haven't yet made a disciple-maker, which is the point.

## This week

Name one person who is a step behind you and hungry to grow. Text them today and ask if they'd want to meet regularly, every other week, over coffee, to grow as followers of Jesus. Set the first appointment now, not someday. Pick one short passage or one good book to start with. Then show up, ask how their soul is, and be honest about your own.

One person, met faithfully over years, can change the trajectory of a whole family line. That is not a small thing done with a small table. It is the largest thing, done one cup at a time.
